units.translation: ... or they converge with the sea and are destroyed, or being driven into the sea they too come to the rocks below Scylla, which are underwater, and are dashed to pieces in this way; then sea-dogs and various other beasts come out and devour the men in the ships. Scylla is thought and said by the poets to have dogs projecting from her sides and chest and to destroy those sailing past her, since from below, from the hollow parts of the rocks on which they dwell, they are seen coming up, and they are suspected of coming out from her chest and sides from within.
c. Charybdis: ... the sea is sucked in by Charybdis. This descent the poet (Od. 12.101 ff.) called Charybdis in Tauromenium.
d. It is below the cape of Sicily called Pelorus, which faces Italy and Scylla. L
e. to go: supply 'you may allow'. Sᵐ
f. Ausonian Scylla: the cave of Scylla was said to be around Italy, which is in the strait. L

g. whom she bore to Phorcys: Acusilaus (2 FGrH 42 J.) says that Scylla is the daughter of Phorcys and Hecate, but Homer (Od. 12.124) says not Hecate but Crataeis. Apollonius followed both. In the Great Ehoiai (Hesiod fr. 150 Rz.²) Scylla is the daughter of Phorbas and Hecate. Stesichorus in his Scylla (fr. 13 B. III 210) says that Scylla is the daughter of †some kind of† Lamia.
834. if indeed of consuming fire: around the strait in the sea there are exhalations of fire, so that even the sea is heated,

as Metrodorus also says in the first book of his On History (184 FGrH 2 J.) and Theophrastus in his Historical Commentaries (fr. 165 Wimmer). And he says that the roar from the islands of Aeolus is heard up to 1000 stades; at any rate around Tauromenium a noise like thunder is heard.

839-41a. I am going away to where the stern cables of the Argo are tied, so that early in the morning they may remember the return, so that I may make them sail away from the land of the Tyrrhenians at dawn. L
b. early in the morning: at the time of dawn, that is, at daybreak; a noun used as an adverb. P
847-48. hyperbolically: for no one can catch the cast of rays or the so-called sparkling, which is a continuous rush of brightness.
850. He called the island of Circe Tyrrhenian because it is near to it. Lᵐ
852. having reached for: having taken hold of. Lᴳ P
856. no longer now on the shores: no longer sit on the shores of the island of Aeaea, which are near the Tyrrhenians, waiting and delaying your voyage. L
859-61a. in fair weather, maidens: all together they come to meet the ship to guard it from the rocks, which are called the Planctae. L
b. they meet: instead of 'they come'. P
